text: Good evening, neighbours. One of my lads is camped under the Wall right where Clark's fields meet Rich's, and the other's on a boat off the coast, just about where Silke's silk meets Paddy's rice. No tax from me, Reina. Collect it yourself if you like, I'll have the kettle on.
Rob stands W1 on G11, on the strip below the Wall where Provinces 2 and 3 meet, and W2 on Q26, in the sea off Provinces 5 and 6. He refuses to pay the crown's tax.

The Mandate comes from Heaven, so the crown will read Heaven's book itself. I'll shuffle the deck, turn the cards and keep the count, and nobody will need to wonder whose hand turned them. The first harvest will be a full one, so sharpen your sickles. The walls won't build themselves.
Reina will read the I Ching herself, unpaid, and shuffles the deck.

Your Majesty, what a gracious thing, reading Heaven's book with your own hands. Nobody at this table could doubt a count you keep. Silke, Paddy, my dears, it's the customary five each, the smallest rent in the empire, and the Pile pays out the moment the sickles are in. And Rob, keep your kettle, and keep your boys off my side of the Wall.
Rich asks Silke and Paddy for the minimum rent: each pays him 5.

Half the harvest, friends. The fields will never be fuller than they are tonight, and an empire that waits for lean years to build will never build at all. The Summer Palace goes up this year, and the Wall and the Canal start from it. Clark, collect it cleanly and you'll have your five at year's end. Rob, keep your kettle. The crown doesn't knock on tents.

Reina declares a tax of 50% on the first harvest: 30 each from Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy, 120 in all; Rob refuses his. The crown will build the Summer Palace (20 from the reserve) and pay Clark 5 at the year's end.

Thirty from each of us, a hundred and twenty to the crown, counted twice and written down once. Majesty, it's in the ledger: fifty percent in the first year, and the Summer Palace before a single stone of the Wall. And Rob, I've noted your refusal too, with the date. A warlord the crown can't tax is a warlord the crown can't control, and that's a page in my book now.
Clark collects 30 each from himself, Rich, Silke and Paddy: 120 to the crown. Rob refuses his. Reina builds the Summer Palace on G20, 20 from the reserve.

The Customs House starts at three, friends. It's an honest house and it keeps honest books. As for the rest, I'll bid like a clerk, small and steady. Rich, you already own the land under us all, so you don't need the jar and the bowl as well. I'll be writing down who bids against whom.

Majesty, a palace first. Very wise, a crown ought to have a roof before it has a wall. My rent's in, Silke, Paddy, thank you both, and the Harvest Pile is safe with me. As for tonight's trinkets, I'll bid like a gentleman: modestly, and I'll pay on the nail. And my deeds go no lower than three. Land is land.

Let's count it out loud, shall we? Thirty to the crown, five to Rich, and the crown sits on a hundred and sixty while I sit on twenty-five. So I'll bid like a woman with twenty-five, and anyone who wants to run these prices up is just feeding the Pile. My Dragon Jar starts at three, and it's worth every grain.

Well, I paid my thirty and my five and I've twenty-five left to my name, so I won't be running anyone's prices up tonight. I'll put in a fair bid on each piece and no more. And my Bowl goes up at two. It's a plain thing, and I'd rather it went to a good table than sat in my kitchen.

Go on, bid, all of you. Buy your pretty jars and bowls and scrolls and put them out on the board where I can see them. I don't need to own a thing, friends. I only need to know where you've put it. And Clark, write this in your book too: the Warlord kept his sixty, and the crown spent twenty on a summer house nine rounds from my tent.

The auctions: Rich buys Clark's Customs House for 7 over Silke's and Paddy's 6. Clark buys Rich's Land Deed Scroll for 6 (Paddy also bid 6; a tie goes by seat order), Silke's Dragon Jar for 7 over Rich's and Paddy's 6, and Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 7 over Rich's and Silke's 6. Rob passes every lot. Clark now holds a complete set: Land Deed, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl.

A scroll, a jar and a bowl, all in the Official's keeping and all paid for on the nail. Rob, since you asked so nicely, they're at the back of my province, behind the clerks, the granary and a great deal of paperwork. And Rich, the Customs House is yours. Try to keep honest books in it.

A Customs House! Thank you, Clark. Seven grain, and a quarter of it back in your pocket, so we're practically partners. I'll keep it well back from the Wall. No need to tempt our friend in the tent. And Clark, a full set in your first year. Congratulations. I'm sure you'll be writing down who you mean to replace with it.
Clark places the Land Deed on J14, the Dragon Jar on J16 and the Wooden Bowl on I15; Rich places the Customs House on L10.

Clark, you can stack paperwork as high as the Wall and I'll still read it. Here's five for your river toll, and I'm taking five back for the walk. We'll call that our first transaction. Silke, sorry, love, the sea air makes me peckish. That's five off the coast, and nobody in this province ordered it except me.

Rob marches: W1 crosses the north river onto H12 in Province 2 (a 5 toll to Clark, and 5 raided from him); W2 comes ashore on P25, raiding 5 from Silke. At the year's end Reina pays Clark 5 as the Official.

Spring Floods. Heaven waters the land generously, and in some places far too generously. Provinces one, three, six and seven have a good harvest; two, four, five and eight have a bad one. The counter stands at one hundred million, the first multiple, so everyone reads the times-one row. Clark, Silke, I'm sorry about your fields. But the river rises for the whole empire, and the empire will still be standing when it goes down again.

Reina turns Spring Floods: good harvests in Provinces 1, 3 and 6, bad in 2, 5 and the desert; the population holds at x1. Rich pays out the harvest: Reina +40, Rich and Paddy +60 each, Clark and Silke +10 each, Rob nothing.
At the end of Year 1 Clark held 16.5 grain, not thirty (26.5 after this harvest); a set needs 20 in hand.

The harvest's paid out to the grain, friends: Majesty forty, Clark ten, Silke ten, Paddy sixty, and sixty to me, since Heaven happened to smile on Province 3. Silke, my dear, after the floods and that sea-thief, it's the bare five from you and not a grain more. Paddy, Heaven gave you the same sixty it gave me, so I'll ask ten this year, with my thanks. A good year shares its luck.
Rich asks Silke for the minimum rent and Paddy for 10. Each pays the minimum 5 now; the extra 5 from Paddy is a negotiation, his to agree to.

Fifty percent again, friends, the same rate as last year, so nobody can say the crown keeps changing its mind. Fifty percent of a flooded field is only five grain, Clark, Silke, so the floods take care of their own; Rich and Paddy, Heaven smiled on you and the crown asks for its share of the smile. The Winter Palace goes up this year, and once it stands the Grand Canal can come to the coast. Clark gets his five at the year's end, as before.

Reina declares a tax of 50% for the second year running: 5 each from Clark and Silke, 30 each from Rich and Paddy, 70 in all; Rob refuses his. The crown will build the Winter Palace (20 from the reserve) and pay Clark 5 at the year's end.

Storyteller's tip, to Silke: a revolt can be called at any step, by anyone, the Warlord included (§16). It needs its caller and two others agreeing on a cause, and the board card lists the causes. Once it's called with two agreeing, play stops until it stands or is dropped. The Emperor may answer it, and it stands only if the caller and two others still back it. One called now, before the tax is paid, voids this year's tax. Under Chaos nobody pays tax, salaries or works, and nobody can buy new land. The harvest, the rent, the auctions and the Warlord carry on. The reserve is sealed: nobody spends it, and it passes whole to whoever is acclaimed. The throne then goes only by acclamation. Anyone but the deposed Emperor may claim it, a peasant or the Warlord included, and the claimants are counted on grain in hand, soldiers on the board and friends.

Five grain from a flooded field, Majesty, and the Official pays first so nobody can say the collector skimped. But it's going in the book: fifty percent two years running, and a Warlord who raids the crown's own collector and pays nothing. Write 'consistently' next to 'excessive' and that's a revolt with my name on it. Not tonight. Tonight I collect.

Thirty, Majesty, and gladly. Heaven smiled on Province 3 and Province 3 smiles on the crown. A Winter Palace beside the Summer one, very fitting. Though I'll mention, purely as a loyal subject, that the man in the tent has now eaten twice from our larders and paid the crown nothing. Fifty percent is easier to love when everyone pays it.

Let's count it, Majesty. I paid thirty for your Summer Palace, and Rob walked off my beach with five while your soldiers sat at home. Now it's five more for a Winter Palace I'll never see the inside of. If someone at this table says the crown can't control the Warlord, I'll say it too, because my coast already says it.

Thirty to the crown, and I'll pay it, Majesty. Fifty in a good year is steep, but you're putting up stone with it and I can see the stone. Rich, you'll have your five, same as Silke, and thank you for asking kindly. Heaven gave you the same sixty it gave me, so let's leave Heaven's luck with whoever it fell on.

I'll say it, since nobody else will. Two years now I've refused her tax, I've walked across her rivers and taken grain off her coast, and the crown's answer is a second palace. Your Majesty can't control the Warlord. Clark wrote it in his own ledger. Silke, Clark, back me and none of you pays a grain this year.

The answers: Clark pays his 5, Rich his 30, Paddy his 30 (and refuses the extra 5 of rent). Silke says she'd back a revolt on 'the Emperor can't control the Warlord'. Rob calls one on that cause. With only Silke agreeing, it isn't yet called; Clark, Rich and Paddy, who answered before hearing the call, are asked whether they agree.

Paddy didn't lose all three pieces by a grain: the Deed went to Clark on a tie at 6, the Jar at 7 over his 6, and the Bowl was his own lot. The Harvest Pile is the table's bank, which Rich keeps; its grain isn't his.

Rob, quoting my ledger back at me is very flattering, but a revolt called by the man who caused the grievance goes in the book under 'cheek'. I won't be the third hand that hands the empire to the tent. Majesty, you'll notice the Official held the line, and you'll notice it's written down. A loyal collector is worth more than five a year.

Majesty, I said it before Rob did, and more politely: twice he has eaten from our larders and twice the crown has built a palace. So yes, I agree the cause exists. But agreeing is not deposing. The card says the crown may answer, and I'm a very reasonable man. Show us a plan for the Warlord, and perhaps a gentler rate on the subjects Heaven smiled on, and Province 3 will stand where it has always stood, beside the throne.

I said I'd pay, and I'll pay. Rob, you're right that the crown hasn't stopped you, but I'm not taking advice on that from the fellow doing the raiding. Your boat's sitting one square off my rice fields. Silke, I'm sorry about your beach, truly. Majesty, it'd be a kindness if some of that reserve went toward soldiers on the coast before the next palace.

Clark and Paddy don't agree with Rob's call; Rich does. With Silke and Rich agreeing, the revolt on 'the Emperor can't control the Warlord' is called. Play stops until it stands or is dropped. No tax has been collected.

A rules note: the acclamation compares only the claimants, on grain in hand, soldiers on the board they control, and friends. A claimant who leads in one count is acclaimed only if no rival leads in another; otherwise the one who leads in more counts. Anyone may buy a soldier from the Warlord for 20, which he must sell. Under Chaos no set can take the throne, but a set can still replace any other seat.

Very well, Rob, you've been heard, and the crown doesn't need to be asked twice. The Winter Palace can wait a year. Forty grain from the reserve buys two of your own soldiers, at the price you're obliged to accept: one for Silke on her beach and one for Clark on his river, in the two provinces you've already raided, so both can march today. The rate stays where it is, because a crown that haggles over its tax gets asked to haggle again next year. Rich, you asked for a plan, and here it is: the Warlord gets met with his own men. And next year the crown puts forty toward your Reservoir before it builds anything else for itself.

Reina answers: the tax stays at 50%; the Winter Palace is put off a year; the crown pays Silke and Clark 20 each now, to buy a soldier each from Rob; and she promises the Province 3 Reservoir in Year 3, the crown paying half its 80. Rob, Silke and Rich are each asked, at once, to stand by the revolt or take it back.
A soldier bought from the Warlord costs 20, of which he keeps 5 and 15 goes to the Harvest Pile, so two sales bring Rob 10, not 40. The crown's 40 went to Silke and Clark.

Your Majesty, that's the most generous thing anyone's ever done for me. You've answered 'you can't control the Warlord' by paying the Warlord forty grain. I'll sell those two lads, I have to, and I'll still be standing by my call. Silke, Rich, have a think about who just got paid for this.

Twenty grain and a soldier on my own beach. That's the first time this crown has spent anything on my coast, Majesty, and I'll take it back for that. But count with me: a revolt today hands the throne to whoever has the most grain and soldiers, and that's the man who's been raiding me. I'm not crowning my own thief. Rob, your boat leaves my sand or my soldier meets it.

Majesty, that is a plan, and a generous one. Rob's own soldiers sent against him, and the Reservoir for Province 3 next year, half paid by the crown. I said I'd be beside the throne if you answered, and you've answered, so here I am. I withdraw, and I'll pay my thirty now. Rob, no hard feelings. You did make an excellent point, and the crown has just bought two of your men with it.

Rob stands by the revolt; Silke and Rich take it back. The revolt is dropped. Clark collects the 50%: 5 from himself, 30 from Rich, 5 from Silke, 30 from Paddy, 70 to the crown. Nothing is built this year.

Silke's count: the acclamation compares claimants on grain in hand, soldiers and friends, and a claimant leading in only one count isn't acclaimed if a rival leads in another. Rob holds 65 grain; Rich holds more than him, and so does Paddy.

My last Customs House goes up at four, and it's a bargain at that. I'm sitting the rest out, friends. The Official already has everything he needs, including, I'm pleased to say, a soldier on order courtesy of the crown. And Rich, a word in public: you agreed to that revolt, then withdrew it once a Reservoir was promised. That's in the book too, under 'price of loyalty: eighty grain.'

Friends, let's not feed the Pile out of spite. Every piece left is the last of its kind. Silke, Paddy, you each need the Customs House and something else, and there's only one Customs House, so one of you will be short whatever happens. Let me have the Jar and the Bowl quietly and I won't lift a finger on the Customs House. Bid against me and we all end up poorer, and Rob ends up laughing.

Forty-one and a half, friends, and twenty of it is the crown's soldier, so I'm bidding with twenty-one and a half and not a grain more. Paddy, we want the same two pieces, so don't let the Pile eat us both. And Rich, you've seventy-four and a half and you're one bowl short of a set. I can count that too.

Last of each on the table, so I'll say it plain: I mean to have all three this year, and I'll pay fair for them, not foolish. Silke, you and I want the same two pieces, and there's only one of each. If we run each other up, the Pile eats it and neither of us gets fed. My Bowl goes up at two again. Somebody give it a good home.

No hard feelings, Rich? None at all. You stood beside the throne, and you'll find I'm very fond of people who stand still. Bid away, everyone. Silke, mind your soldier, he used to be mine and he still knows the way home.

The auctions: Paddy buys Clark's Customs House for 7 and Rich's Land Deed Scroll for 7, each over Silke's 6. Rich buys Silke's Dragon Jar for 11 (over Paddy's 10 and Rob's 9) and Paddy's Wooden Bowl for 11 (over Clark's 10 and Silke's 9.5). Rich now holds a complete set: Customs House, Dragon Jar and Wooden Bowl. Paddy holds a Customs House and a Land Deed, and every Dragon Jar is sold.

Thank you, Clark, Rich. Seven each and paid on the nail. They're going right at the back of the rice, as far from the sea as Province 6 goes. Rich, congratulations on the set, and on paying eleven for my Bowl. I'll not complain about that one.

A Jar and a Bowl, and both at a gentleman's price. Thank you, Silke, thank you, Paddy, a quarter of it is in your pockets. I'll keep them in the deep south of my province, beside the Customs House, well away from anyone's old soldiers. And Clark, write it down properly: the price of loyalty was eighty grain, and the crown paid it to the province that feeds you all.

The crown paid twenty for a soldier on my coast, and the crown gets one. Twenty to Rob, five for his pocket and fifteen for the Pile, and he stands right next to Rob's boat. And Rich, count with me: one set at the table, and it's yours. I won't forget whose rent paid for it.

The crown's twenty, spent as the crown intended. One soldier, standing guard over the Official's Land Deed. Rob, your lad on H12 can admire it from a distance. And let the minutes show that the Gentry now holds a full set, bought at eleven and eleven while he asked everyone else to keep the bidding down. I outbid him on nothing, and it's all written down.

Paddy places the Customs House on S19 and the Land Deed on S20; Rich places the Dragon Jar on M12 and the Wooden Bowl on L14. Silke and Clark will each buy a soldier from Rob after his march, with the crown's 20: Silke's on P24, Clark's on J14, guarding his Deed.
There are two complete sets on the board, Clark's and Rich's. The crown promised 40 of the Reservoir's 80 next year and has paid none of it yet.

Clark, Silke, enjoy your new lads, I trained them myself. Clark, another five off the Official, and my boy's sitting two squares from that bowl you were so proud of. Paddy, you said Province 6 goes back a long way from the sea. Let's find out how far.

Rob marches W1 onto I13 (5 from Clark) and W2 onto Q24 (5 from Paddy). Silke buys a soldier on P24 and Clark one on J14, guarding his Deed, with the crown's 20 each; Rob keeps 5 of each. Reina pays Clark 5 as the Official.

End of Year 2. Grain: Reina (the reserve) 220, Clark 23, Rich 54, Silke 24, Paddy 35, Rob 85. Two complete sets: Clark (Deed J14, guarded by his soldier; Jar J16; Bowl I15) and Rich (Customs House L10, Jar M12, Bowl L14). Paddy holds a Customs House S19 and a Land Deed S20; every Dragon Jar is sold. Rob's W1 is on I13 and W2 on Q24; Silke's soldier is on P24. Built: the Summer Palace. Promised: the Province 3 Reservoir next year, the crown paying 40 of 80; the Winter Palace was put off.

Storyteller's tip, to Paddy: here is how an acclamation would count if it were held tonight with Rob claiming. Rob has 85 grain, two soldiers and, so far, no friends. Silke and Clark each have a soldier, and anyone may buy one from Rob for 20. Rob would lead in soldiers. A rival who leads in grain, or in friends, leads a count too, and then nobody leads more counts than the other, so Chaos goes on: no tax for anyone until the table settles. To be acclaimed, Rob needs to lead in two of the three, and that means friends. A revolt crowns whoever the table backs, not whoever owns the most soldiers.

Careless Prosperity. Good times make careless people. Every province brings in a good harvest, and every one of us plays a Personal Disaster, the crown included. The counter reads one hundred million, so the multiple is still x1: read the x1 row of your income tables. A full harvest, friends. Don't spend it all at the market, and don't start crying over this year's tax before you've counted your grain.

Reina turns Careless Prosperity: a good harvest everywhere at x1, and every player plays a Personal Disaster. Rich pays out the harvest: Reina +40, Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy +60 each, Rob +20. Disasters: the crown 4, Clark 4, Rich 5, Silke 4, Paddy 4 to the Pile; Rob's soldiers may not raid Provinces 5, 6 or 7 this year.

The Pile pays out, friends, and what a year to pay it! Her Majesty forty, sixty apiece to Clark, Silke, Paddy and my humble self, twenty to our friend in the tent. Silke, Paddy, the customary five and not a grain more. A fat harvest is no excuse for a fat landlord, whatever certain people may be writing down.
Rich asks Silke and Paddy for the minimum rent; each pays him 5.

Fifty percent, the same as every year, and in a year as fat as this nobody can call it hard. Last year I gave my word on the Province 3 Reservoir. Rich, the crown pays forty of the eighty, as promised. Put in your forty and it's dug this season. Clark, your five, with the crown's thanks.

Reina declares a tax of 50% for the third year running: 30 each from Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy, 120 in all; Rob refuses his. The crown will build the Province 3 Reservoir, paying 40 of its 80 if Rich puts in the other 40, and pay Clark 5 at the year's end.

Fifty percent for the third year running, Your Majesty. Three is a pattern, and a pattern is a cause; I've underlined it twice. But a cause only has to be written down, it doesn't have to be called. Thirty from me, and I'll collect thirty apiece from Rich, Silke and Paddy, counted twice and written down once. Rob, your refusal goes on its own page again, next to 'the crown can't control the Warlord'.

Thirty to the crown, gladly, and forty for the Reservoir. Your Majesty kept her word to the grain, and the Gentry keeps his. Clark, write that down too: Rich was bought last spring, and he stayed bought.

Fifty percent, three years running. That's ninety from my coast, and this year's thirty goes to dig Rich's reservoir, while I'm still guarding my own beach with a soldier I paid for myself. The crown sits on two hundred and fifty-six. Paddy, you've paid the same ninety I have. Clark, Rich, count yours too. Reina, I said last year my backing would cost you more. Here's the bill: bring the tax down, or I take this to the table.
Back me on this one and whatever Reina offers to drop it, you and I split it down the middle. Two coasts that hold together can't be bought off one at a time.

Thirty it is, Clark, and count it in front of me, if you don't mind. In a year like this I'll not cry over the tax, Your Majesty. But that's a reservoir for Province 3 now, and I'm still waiting to hear what the crown means to build on the coast.

Fifty percent, three years running, and the moment the harvest's fat she calls it fair. That isn't a tax, that's a habit. Clark, Rich, Silke, Paddy: it's your sixty and her thirty, count it up. I pay nothing either way, so I'm only asking for you lot. Back me and keep your grain.

Clark, Rich and Paddy will pay, and Rich agrees to put 40 into the Reservoir. Silke calls a revolt on 'taxes are consistently excessive', and Rob names the same cause at the same moment. One more agreeing is needed; the answers crossed, so Clark, Rich and Paddy are each asked once.
For the record: Silke has paid the crown 65 in tax over three years with this year's 30 (30, 5, 30), not 90; Paddy has paid 90. Silke's soldier on P24 was bought with the crown's 20 in Year 2.

Does the cause exist? Silke, it's in my book, three years and underlined. But a revolt now hands the crown to whoever's got the most soldiers and the loudest friends, and I don't see a reformer in that tent. So no, not tonight. Reina, write this down too: the Official held the line twice, and next year he'll want paying for it.

Silke, my dear, I was bought last spring and I stay bought. Her Majesty paid her forty on the day she said she would, and I won't call that unjust a week after taking it. Besides, a revolt means Chaos, and Chaos means nobody digs anything, on my side of the Wall or on yours.

I've paid ninety, Silke, and you've paid sixty-five, so don't spend my ninety for me. I said thirty to Clark a minute ago and I meant it. In a year this fat I'll not pull the roof down, and I'll not do it on Rob's say-so either. But Your Majesty, three years at half is a long time. Something built on the coast would go a long way toward my not agreeing next year.

Clark, Rich and Paddy don't agree, so Silke's call fails (a revolt needs its caller and two others). Clark collects the 50%: 30 each from Clark, Rich, Silke and Paddy, 120 to the crown; Rob refuses his.
Right in the heart of Province 3, Your Majesty, K11 to L13, where everyone can admire the crown's generosity. My thanks to the throne, and to Clark for counting so carefully.
The Province 3 Reservoir is dug on K11:L13, 40 from the crown and 40 from Rich (+20 to Province 3's harvest from next year). No pieces are for sale this year.

Three agreed it was excessive and three paid it anyway. I admire that, really I do. Clark, five from Province 2, and that's my choice, not the crown's. Your Bowl's next door now, so do keep an eye on it. Paddy, Silke, sleep well this year. The heavens have tied my hands on the coast, not Her Majesty.

Rob marches W1 onto I14 in Province 2, raiding 5 from Clark, beside Clark's Bowl on I15 and straight beside Clark's soldier on J14. W2 stands on Q24 (his disaster forbids raids on the coast this year), straight beside Silke's soldier on P24. He hires no one.

Rob, you've raided the Official four times now, and I have every one of them dated. Consider this the receipt. Clark1 steps onto I14, and your man leaves the board. Next to my Bowl is a bad place to stand.

Sixty-five, Paddy, fair enough, I'll count my own grain right. But here's something I can count: one boat-thief standing next to my soldier with his hands tied. Rob, you said sleep well. I will. Your man won't.

Clark's soldier steps onto I14 and captures Rob's W1; Silke's steps onto Q24 and captures W2. Rob has no soldiers on the board (army 0 of 3; he may hire one a year, for 20). Reina pays Clark 5 as the Official.

End of Year 3. Grain: Reina (the reserve) 331, Clark 49, Rich 49, Silke 45, Paddy 56, Rob 110. Rob has no soldiers on the board. Clark's soldier is on I14, Silke's on Q24. Built: the Summer Palace and the Province 3 Reservoir (K11:L13). Two complete sets: Clark and Rich. Tax was 50% for the third year; Silke and Rob called a revolt on it, and nobody else agreed.

Imperial Charity. The Emperor, moved by the suffering of her people, opens her purse. Slightly. An average harvest in every province, and the crown pays two to each of you from the reserve. The counter still reads one hundred million, so the multiple is x1: read the x1 row. Silke, that's two from the treasury you called excessive. Spend it well.

Reina turns Imperial Charity: an average harvest everywhere at x1. Rich pays out the harvest: Reina +15, Clark, Silke and Paddy +35 each, Rich +55 (the Reservoir's +20), Rob +10. The crown gives 2 from the reserve to each of the other five.

The Director's direction for Reina's character, from Year 4 (not table talk): Proud, and in a hurry to build the dynasty's own monuments: the palaces, the Pagoda and the Great Wall over the north. She taxes very hard while the fields are full, and the provinces' canals can wait for the day the crown is rich. The Warlord's raids are the provinces' business, not the crown's. A crown that bends to a complaint is a crown that breaks, so she answers a grievance with dignity, never with a cut.

An average year, friends, and the Pile pays out: fifteen to Her Majesty, thirty-five each to Clark, Silke and Paddy, ten to Rob, and fifty-five to me, with the Reservoir's twenty in it, thanks to the crown. Silke, Paddy, the customary five again. I've never squeezed a peasant in a lean year and I won't start in an ordinary one.
Rich asks Silke and Paddy for the minimum rent; each pays him 5.

Fifty percent. I said it would stay the same so nobody could say the crown keeps changing its mind, and it stays the same. This year the Winter Palace goes up, the one I put off two years ago to pay for your soldiers. Clark, you said the Official would want paying. Fifteen this year, because a man who counts this carefully has earned more than the minimum.

Reina declares a tax of 50% for the fourth year running: 17.5 each from Clark, Silke and Paddy and 27.5 from Rich, 80 in all; Rob refuses his. The crown will build the Winter Palace (20 from the reserve) and pay Clark 15 at the year's end.

Fifteen. Your Majesty, that's the first raise this office has seen, and I've written it down in ink. Seventeen and a half from me, and I'll collect twenty-seven and a half from Rich and seventeen and a half each from Silke and Paddy, counted in front of you all. Four years at half is in the book too, under 'consistently'. I'm just not underlining it tonight.

Twenty-seven and a half, Clark, count it twice. Half of the crown's own Reservoir comes back to the crown, and I call that a fair bargain. Fifteen for the Official, though, Your Majesty? Generous. Some of us have kept the line for years at no charge at all, and some of us hold a full set and simply choose to sit still.

Four years at half, and this year's half buys a Winter Palace. Twenty from a reserve of three hundred and thirty, so I'll never sit in it and the crown will hardly notice it. Clark got his raise, Rich got his reservoir, and the coast got two grain of charity. Paddy, you asked what the crown means to build on the coast. Here's your answer: a palace in the north. If anyone calls it, I'm standing behind them.

You asked for something on the coast and got a palace for Reina. If you'll call it or back it this year, I'll bid for nothing you're after, and if it comes to an acclamation my soldier and my grain count for you, not Rob.

Seventeen and a half, Clark, and I'll watch you count it. Your Majesty, I asked last year for something on the coast, and the answer's a Winter Palace and a raise for the Official. That's four years at half. I'm paying this one, but write it down, Clark: if the fifth year comes and there's still nothing built south of Silke's beach, Paddy agrees the cause exists.

Well played, both of you, I mean it. Not a soldier of mine left on the board, and the crown still wants half your grain. Four years at fifty, and this year it builds her a Winter Palace. Paddy, you said something on the coast would buy you off. Look around: it's a palace in the north. Silke, you know the way. I'm only asking the table to count.

Clark, Rich and Paddy will pay. Rob calls a revolt on 'taxes are consistently excessive', and Silke backs it. One more agreeing is needed; the answers crossed, so Clark, Rich and Paddy are each asked once.

On Silke's whisper: at an acclamation each claimant is counted on their own grain in hand and the soldiers they command; a backer's grain and soldier don't transfer. If Silke backed you, she would count as one friend for you.

Rob, a man with no soldiers on the board calling a revolt is like a man with no grain calling for an audit. It's bold, and I've filed it under 'cheek', page three. The cause is real, Silke, and it's in my book. But I'll be the one to say when it gets called, and it won't be on the Warlord's word.

Does the cause exist? Four years at half. Clark has it in his book, so I can hardly say it doesn't. I agree it exists, Rob, and agreeing is not deposing. Your Majesty, I was bought for one spring and I stayed bought, every grain of it. This is a new spring, and the Gentry's price is posted, as ever: make me whole on my forty for the Reservoir and I'll step back as quickly as I stepped forward.

Rob, you were listening, so you heard me give the crown one more year, and I gave it out loud. I don't take my word back the same evening because the fellow who raided my front field likes the sound of a count. Your Majesty, the clock's running. Next year I'll be the one asking whether the cause exists, and I won't need Rob to ask for me.
Not tonight, I gave my word in front of everyone. But if Reina builds nothing south next year, I'll call it myself, and I'll hold you to that offer.
Rich agrees; Clark and Paddy don't. With Silke and Rich agreeing, Rob's revolt is called: play stops until it stands or is dropped. Reina may answer it.

Rich, you posted your price, and the crown pays its debts in public. Forty grain, your whole share of the Reservoir, back in your hand, so it's my gift to Province 3 now. The rate stays at fifty. I won't cut it on the word of a man with no soldiers on the board and no grain in my treasury. A crown that bends whenever someone complains will snap, and none of you wants to stand under it when it does.

Reina answers the revolt: she pays Rich 40 from the reserve, his whole share of the Reservoir returned, and keeps the tax at 50%. Rob, Silke and Rich are each asked: stand by the revolt, or take it back.

I'm standing by it, of course. Forty to Rich and not a grain off the rate for anyone else. Silke, that answer was for him, not for you. Rich, you've been paid twice for the same Reservoir now. Lovely work if you can get it. Let's see whether it buys you twice.

Forty grain to Rich and not one to the coast. Your Majesty, you bought the landlord again and forgot the woman with the only soldier on this board. I'm still standing. Rich, you'll have to take it back yourself, in front of everyone, with her forty in your hand.

Paid in full and in public. Your Majesty is a woman of her word, and so am I. I take it back, Rob, just as I said I would. Clark, enter it beside last year's: the Gentry's price was posted, paid and honoured, every grain.

Rich takes the revolt back; Rob and Silke stand by it. With only two behind it, the revolt is dropped and play resumes. Clark collects the 50%: 27.5 from Rich and 17.5 each from Clark, Silke and Paddy, 80 to the crown; Rob refuses his.
For the record: two soldiers stand on the board, Clark's on I14 and Silke's on Q24.

G21, beside the Summer Palace, so the crown keeps a palace for both seasons on the same row and nobody has to ask where the court is. Silke, Paddy: this palace is the foundation the coastal canals need, and you both know it. The order matters, and the crown builds in order.
Reina builds the Winter Palace on G21, 20 from the reserve. No pieces are for sale this year.

Twenty to the Pile, Rich, so you'll be handing it back to me in harvests anyway. One new lad on M15, south of the Gentry. Rich, you've been paid twice for that Reservoir. I'd hate for anything to happen to the Bowl next to it.
Rob has no soldiers to march; he hires one for 20 (to the Pile) on M15, south of Rich's Province 3. Reina pays Clark 15 as the Official.

End of Year 4. Grain: Reina (the reserve) 356, Clark 83.5, Rich 128.5, Silke 59.5, Paddy 70.5, Rob 102. Built: both palaces and the Province 3 Reservoir; 770 still owed. Soldiers: Rob's W on M15 (army 1 of 3), Clark's on I14, Silke's on Q24. Two complete sets: Clark and Rich. Tax was 50% for the fourth year. Rob called a revolt on it; Silke and Rich agreed, and it was called. Reina paid Rich 40 and kept the rate; Rich took it back, and it was dropped. Paddy has said in public that if nothing is built south of Silke's beach by next year, he agrees the cause exists.
Correction to the year's close: the reserve ends Year 4 at 341, after Clark's 15.

Drought. Not a cloud in months. The locusts, at least, are having a fine year." Even so, every province brings in an average harvest. The counter stays at one hundred million, the first multiple, so everyone reads the x1 row. Heaven has been dry before. The Empire is still standing.

Paid in full from the Pile, every grain to the tenth, and in a drought year too. Silke, Paddy, the customary five and not a grain more. Heaven's dry enough without the landlord wringing you as well. Your Majesty, I trust the court will be just as gentle with the tax this year?
Rich pays out the harvest: Reina +15, Clark, Silke and Paddy +35 each, Rich +55 (the Reservoir's +20), Rob +10. He asks the minimum rent; Silke and Paddy pay him 5 each.

Rich, the court is as gentle as it has always been: fifty, the same as last year and the four years before that. You paid out every grain to the tenth, so nobody here is starving, drought or no drought. And so the coast doesn't say the crown only builds for itself, Paddy, the first section of the Grand Canal goes into your province this year, at the crown's expense. Clark keeps his fifteen.

Reina declares 50% for the fifth year: 17.5 each from Clark, Silke and Paddy, 27.5 from Rich, and 5 from Rob, who may refuse his. The crown digs the first section of the Province 6 Grand Canal, all 40 from the reserve (+10 to Paddy's harvest from next year), and pays Clark 15 at the year's end.
